title: Perspective

learn.summary: Linear perspective — codified by Brunelleschi in Florence around 1420 — is the geometry of how parallel lines converge to vanishing points on the horizon (your eye level). It transformed Western art in a generation. You need working fluency in one- and two-point perspective; everything else is refinement.

do: Stand in a hallway or street and hold a pencil against the visible edges of walls and windows — confirm they all aim at a single point at your eye level.

children.title: One-Point Perspective

learn.summary: One-point perspective applies when a box form faces you directly: verticals stay vertical, horizontals stay horizontal, and all depth lines converge to a single vanishing point. It is the perspective of hallways, railroad tracks, and streets shot head-on. The vanishing point always sits on the horizon line, which is always your eye level — internalize that equivalence.

do: Draw your view down a hallway or street in one-point perspective this week, ruling every depth edge back to one marked vanishing point.

children.title: Two-Point Perspective

learn.summary: When you view a box from an angle, its two visible wall directions converge to two vanishing points, both on the horizon — usually far apart, often off the page. Keep them wide: points too close together produce the telltale distorted 'fisheye box.' Two-point handles most buildings, interiors, and furniture, making it the workhorse of sketching.

do: Draw the corner view of a building or a large box in two-point perspective, placing both vanishing points on a taped-on extension of your page.

children.title: Ellipses

learn.summary: A circle seen at an angle is an ellipse, defined by its degree (how open it is) and its minor axis, which must align with the cylinder's central axis — the rule that makes mugs, wheels, and cups sit correctly. Ellipses get rounder as they move away from your eye level. Freehand ellipse control is pure mileage: thousands of repetitions, ideally inside guide boxes.

do: Draw a stack of five cylinders from eye level down to tabletop level, making each ellipse progressively rounder, and check every minor axis against the center line.

children.title: Three-Point Perspective

learn.summary: Add a third vanishing point above or below the horizon and verticals converge too — the drama of looking up at a skyscraper or down from a rooftop. It is two-point plus tilt, so master two-point first. Comic artists lean on it for heroic worm's-eye and bird's-eye shots.

do: Draw one tall building from a worm's-eye view with verticals converging to a third point high above the page.
